summary: This document gives guidelines for personal interaction in the Internet Engineering Task Force. They recognize the diversity of participants, emphasize mutual respect, and stress the broad applicability of IETF work. It updates earlier conduct guidelines.

eli5.summary: This is a short list of rules for being respectful when working with others on Internet standards.

questions: what are the ietf guidelines for conduct
how to report ietf conduct violations
subtitle: A short code of conduct for the people who write Internet standards: be respectful, argue ideas not people, and think about the whole Internet.

tldr.problem: IETF work depends on cooperation among a diverse range of people with different ideas and communication styles, and it needs shared expectations for how they treat each other.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets out four guidelines: extend respect and courtesy, keep discussions impersonal, devise solutions for the global Internet, and come prepared to contribute.
tldr.outcome: It replaces RFC 3184 as BCP 54 and adds text saying the IETF strives to treat every person with dignity, decency, and respect.

today: RFC 7154 is a Best Current Practice published in March 2014. It obsoletes RFC 3184 and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why the IETF Has Conduct Guidelines
sections.content:
The work of the IETF relies on cooperation among a diverse range of people with different ideas and communication styles. Through these guidelines the IETF strives to create and maintain an environment in which every person is treated with dignity, decency, and respect.

Participants are expected to behave in a professional manner while they develop interoperable technologies for the Internet, whether they build consensus in person or through email discussions. If conflicts arise, they are resolved according to the procedures in RFC 2026.

This document obsoletes RFC 3184, of which it is an updated version.
sections.eli5: Lots of different people work together on the Internet, so they agree on how to treat each other. Everybody should feel respected.

sections.title: Respect and Courtesy
sections.content:
The first guideline says IETF participants extend respect and courtesy to their colleagues at all times. People come from diverse origins and backgrounds and may have different expectations or assumptions. Regardless of those differences, participants treat colleagues with respect as persons, especially when it is difficult to agree with them: treat other participants as you would like to be treated.

The guideline also deals with language. English is the de facto language of the IETF, but it is not the native language of many participants. All participants, particularly those with English as a first language, attempt to accommodate others by communicating clearly, including speaking slowly and limiting the use of slang. When English is difficult to understand, participants make a sincere effort to understand each other and engage in conversation to clarify what was meant.
sections.eli5: Treat other people the way you want to be treated. If someone is still learning your language, talk slowly and skip the slang.

sections.title: Impersonal Discussion
sections.content:
The second guideline is that IETF participants have impersonal discussions. Ideas are disputed by reasoned argument rather than through intimidation or personal attack.

Participants are encouraged to provide data and facts for their standpoints, so that the rest of the participants, who are sitting on the sidelines watching the discussion, can form an opinion. The RFC adds that discussion is easier when the response to a simple question is a polite answer, and cites a talk titled "Miss Manners meets the IETF".

Appendix C notes that this guideline was reworded as a positive statement compared with RFC 3184.
sections.eli5: If you disagree, talk about the idea, not about the person. Bring facts so the people listening can decide for themselves.

sections.title: Solutions for the Global Internet
sections.content:
The third guideline is that participants devise solutions for the global Internet that meet the needs of diverse technical and operational environments. It restates the IETF mission: to produce high-quality, relevant technical and engineering documents that influence the way people design, use, and manage the Internet so as to make the Internet work better. The IETF puts its emphasis on technical competence, rough consensus, and individual participation, and needs to be open to competent input from any source.

Participants are asked to use their best engineering judgment to find the best solution for the whole Internet, not just for any particular network, technology, vendor, or user. They also bear in mind that "scaling is the ultimate problem", since many ideas that work on a small scale fail that test. No one shall ever knowingly contribute advice or text that would make a standard technically inferior.
sections.eli5: When you help design something for the whole world, pick what works best for everyone, not just for your own team or company.

sections.title: Coming Prepared
sections.content:
The fourth guideline is that individuals are prepared to contribute to the ongoing work of the group. Participants follow the intellectual property guidelines in BCP 79 (RFC 3979) and read the relevant Internet-Drafts, RFCs, and email archives to become familiar with the technology under discussion.

Working Group sessions run on a very limited time schedule, so participants sometimes have to limit their questions. The work continues on the mailing list, where questions can be asked and answered. Information about a Working Group, including its charter and milestones, is available on the IETF datatracker site or from the Working Group Chair.
sections.eli5: Read the background before you join the conversation, and save extra questions for the group's mailing list when the meeting runs out of time.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The guidelines for conduct do not directly affect the security of the Internet. The RFC does note an expectation, though, that no one shall ever knowingly contribute advice or text that may adversely affect the security of the Internet without describing all known or foreseen risks and threats to potential implementers and users that they are aware of.
sections.eli5: If you know your idea could make the Internet less safe, you must say so clearly instead of keeping it quiet.

sections.title: Reporting and Consequences
sections.content:
An individual can report transgressions of the guidelines to the IETF Chair or the IESG (Appendix A). The document itself does not discuss measures that can be taken against a participant who transgresses them (Appendix B).

It points to existing mechanisms instead. RFC 2418 lets a Working Group Chair refuse the floor to an individual who is unprepared or covering inappropriate material, or who is disrupting the process. RFC 3683 describes a "posting rights" action that removes the posting rights of an individual, and RFC 3934 describes a way for a Working Group Chair to suspend posting privileges of a disruptive individual for a short period of time.
sections.eli5: If someone breaks the rules, you can tell the leaders. This document does not list punishments, but other documents explain how a meeting chair can stop someone from talking or posting.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 3184
sections.content:
Appendix C lists what changed from RFC 3184:

  • Added text about the IETF striving to create an environment in which every person is treated with dignity, decency, and respect.
  • Added text about contributing advice or text that may affect the security of the Internet.
  • Removed the recommendation that newcomers should not interfere with the ongoing process, because it can be read as discouraging newcomers from participating.
  • Replaced the text about the goal of the IETF with text about the mission statement and what the IETF puts its emphasis on.
  • Removed the "think globally" text because its meaning was not clear.
  • Clarified the text about English as a first language.
  • Reworded the impersonal discussion guideline as a positive statement.
sections.eli5: The authors cleaned up the old rules: they added kinder wording, removed a line that might scare off newcomers, and made a few unclear parts clearer.

items.title: Respect and courtesy
items.text: Treat colleagues as you would like to be treated, and communicate clearly.

items.title: Impersonal discussion
items.text: Dispute ideas with reasoned argument, not intimidation or personal attack.

items.title: Global solutions
items.text: Find the best solution for the whole Internet, not one network or vendor.

items.title: Be prepared
items.text: Read the drafts, RFCs and archives before contributing.
